paper_title: Seeing Right, Writing Wrong: Where Short Chain-of-Thought Breaks Spatial VQA

sections.title: Abstract
sections.content: Asking a vision-language model (VLM) to think step by step often makes it worse at spatial questions, even though the image stays in context. We show that short chain-of-thought (CoT) turns a perception problem into a transcription problem. Once a VLM writes a spatial relation, its answer follows that sentence instead of the image, so whether CoT helps or hurts depends largely on whether the written relation is more accurate than answering directly. Studying 15 open VLMs (2B-38B) and six frontier closed models, we rule out token count, turn format, and visual forgetting in open models and trace the failure through three stages. First, writing re-weights visual cues, weakening a "lower is closer" shortcut in all 13 open models tested but also discarding valid cues, which produces false relations. Second, the written text takes over. With the model's own conclusion-removed rationale held fixed, swapping in an opposite-depth image moves the answer by 2-9 points on rendered twins (vs. up to 77 for direct answers) and by 3.0-3.4 points on average on natural photographs (vs. 20.5-69.6). Third, the concluding sentence can invert even a true relation, mainly on converse questions. Together, false relations and conclusion mis-mapping account for four in five CoT losses. Scale does not remove this bottleneck: Qwen3-VL-32B shows the same pattern. Frontier closed models are not hurt: they write relations as accurately as they answer, and three of six re-check the image after writing. The three queried with reasoning off lock in like open models, so re-grounding co-occurs with answer-turn reasoning; we identify answer-step re-grounding as the step open VLMs lack. In a single-model pilot, fine-tuning on fixed rationales with image-determined labels restores it on natural photographs. We open-sourced all our datasets and code at https://ming-zch.github.io/seeing-right-writing-wrong.

sections.content: 1. Introduction Asking vision-language model (VLM) to think step by step often makes it worse at spatial questions, even though the image stays in context. We show that short chain-of-thought (CoT) turns perception problem into transcription problem. Once VLM writes spatial relation, its answer follows that sentence instead of the image, so whether CoT helps or hurts depends largely on whether the written relation is more accurate than answering directly. Studying 15 open VLMs (2B38B) and six frontier closed models, we rule out token count, turn format, and visual forgetting in open models and trace the failure through three stages. First, writing reweights visual cues, weakening lower is closer shortcut in all 13 open models tested but also discarding valid cues, which produces false relations. Second, the written text takes over. With the models own conclusion-removed rationale held fixed, swapping in an opposite-depth image moves the answer by 29 points on rendered twins (vs. up to 77 for direct answers) and by 3.03.4 points on average on natural photographs (vs. 20.569.6). Third, the concluding sentence can invert even true relation, mainly on converse questions. Together, false relations and conclusion mis-mapping account for four in five CoT losses. Scale does not remove this bottleneck: Qwen3-VL-32B shows the same pattern. Frontier closed models are not hurt: they write relations as accurately as they answer, and three of six re-check the image after writing. The three queried with reasoning off lock in like open models, so re-grounding co-occurs with answerturn reasoning; we identify answer-step re-grounding as the step open VLMs lack. In single-model pilot, fine-tuning on fixed rationales with image-determined labels restores it on natural photographs. We open-sourced all our datasets and code at https://ming-zch.github.io/seeing-right-writingwrong. Writing intermediate steps helps language models reason [47], yet on spatial questions about images, chainof-thought (CoT) prompting and reasoning tuning often lower accuracy [23, 33, 50], and reinforcement-learning studies find that explicit thinking need not aid visual perception [21, 30, 52]. Even though the image remains in context throughout generation, three mechanisms could explain this drop: extra tokens or turn formatting may shift the answer distribution, generated prose may weaken access to the image [10, 39, 40], or the semantic content of what the model writes may alter the decision. We test these explanations on binary depth and spatial questions across 15 open VLMs (2B38B: seven core instruct models up to 8B, three reasoning-tuned models, three 32B38B instruct models, and Qwen3-VL 2B/4B ladder) and six frontier closed models (Sec. 3). Turn-closed filler of the rationales length keeps all eight main-pool open models (the core seven and Qwen3-VL-8B-Thinking) within 2.3 points of direct answering (Direct), and re-showing the image or question after the rationale recovers at most 0.8 points each on the main pool (Sec. 4). Instead, the semantic content of the rationale drives the change. Much like verbal overshadowing in humans, where describing face impairs its later recognition [33, 38], short CoT turns perception problem into transcription problem  (Fig. 1)  . Once VLM writes spatial relation, it reads its final answer from that sentence rather than from the image, so CoT helps or hurts largely according to whether the written relation is more accurate than Direct, minus conclusion-mapping cost. We trace this handoff with forced readout, the probability of the correct option at the prefix Answer: ( appended after the question (Direct) or after any sentence of the rationale, and find three stages: 1. Stage 1: writing re-weights visual cues (Sec. 5). Writing weakens lower is closer height shortcut in all 13 open models (Fig. 3a), which helps shortcut-reliant models on cue-balanced scenes, but it can also lose valid cue that Direct reads. Of the 3,014 items where Direct Figure 1. Seeing right, writing wrong. (b) First two-object claims in Synthetic Depth rationales (all 500 scenes; six models) judged false by two image-conditioned judges (consensus, Wilson CIs) on D+C vs. D+C+ items. (c) Twin image effect (in points, where 100 means the answer follows the image) before vs. after relation is written. Middle: unselected Direct vs. the models own conclusion-removed rationale Rcut held fixed (seven-model means; Tabs. 1, 5 and 6). Bottom: three closed models on the hard set (Direct at lowest reasoning vs. own conclusion-removed rationale held fixed; Tab. 13). is right and CoT wrong (D+C) on our three occlusion sets, 57% end in false written relation (Fig. 3b), typically an occlusion misreading that affirms the queried subject, even while mid-layer probe at the relation word still decodes the true depth order. 2. Stage 2: the written text takes over (Secs. 5 and 6). coherent reasoner should follow its own text, so the informative test is whether the image still matters after relation is written. In our primary unselected fixedrationale swaps, holding each models own conclusionremoved rationale (Rcut) fixed reduces the twin image effect to 2.08.9 points across the core seven models (vs. up to 76.5 under Direct), lowers the mirror effect on natural photographs from 69.6 to 3.4, and lowers the occlusion effect on COCO object composites from 20.5 to 3.0. Conversely, editing the first written claim to the true relation beats Direct by 14.334.9 points in five of six models. Along D+C rationales, the forced readout stays right until single commit sentence j, which usually states spatial relation that contradicts the image (88.0% of audited Synthetic Depth cases). In an exploratory, selection-constrained prefix swap around that commit sentence, swapping in the twin moves the readout by 64.686.9 points before it versus 3.03.7 after it in Qwen3-VL-8B and -32B (an unselected D+C+ control similarly falls from 47.1 26.9 and 70.8 32.6 after the first true relation, and to 7.8 and 9.6 two sentences later; Tab. S14). 3. Stage 3: the conclusion can mis-map true relation (Sec. 6). Another 24% of losses write true relation and then answer the wrong option, mostly on converse questions (29.5% errors vs. 2.4% on restatements). Together, false relation or conclusion mis-mapping accounts for four in five CoT losses, where the model sees right under Direct but writes wrong in CoT. Separating writtenrelation accuracy from the answer step explains when CoT helps or hurts (Sec. 7), and scaling model size alone does not remove this bottleneck (Qwen3-VL-32B exhibits the same pattern). Frontier closed models show that text lock-in is avoidable (Sec. 8): when swapped image contradicts their own correct written relation, Claude Opus 5.5, GPT-6-Astra, and Gemini-4-Argon follow the image (Claude and GPT reason at the answer turn, while Gemini reports no reasoning counts), whereas Qwen3.8-Max, DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash, and HY4 (queried with reasoning off) lock onto their text like the open models. While label-free inference-time interventions do not beat Direct on average out of sample, single-model pre-specified LoRA pilot indicates that answer-step re-grounding is learnable on natural photographs (Sec. 9). Our main contributions are: controlled diagnosis of why short CoT hurts spatial VQA across 15 open and six closed VLMs, with controls in open models that rule out token count, turn format, and 2 visual forgetting (Sec. 4). sentence-level account of where rationales turn against the image, verified with forced readouts, claim edits, attention knockouts, and fixed-rationale image swaps on rendered scenes and natural photographs (Secs. 5 and 6). An accounting decomposition (written-relation accuracy versus the answer step) that explains when CoT helps or hurts across synthetic benchmarks and larger or reasoning-tuned open cohorts, predicts the out-of-sample CoTDirect change on natural depth with mean absolute error of 1.3 points, and predicts the sign on held-out natural-object composites (Sec. 7). Evidence that lock-in is avoidable and re-grounding is learnable, contrasting frontier closed models with open VLMs (Sec. 8), evaluating label-free interventions, and showing in single-model pre-specified LoRA pilot that fine-tuning on fixed rationales with image-determined labels restores answer-step re-grounding on natural photographs (Sec. 9 and Tab. 15). 2. Related Work CoT and visual perception. Strong language skills do not ensure accurate perception [41, 42]: VLMs confuse spatial prepositions [22], lose metric memory in video and 3D CoT [44, 50, 51], and gain little or lose accuracy from thinking in RL and evaluation [21, 30, 52]. Across 13 spatial benchmarks, CoT and reasoning tuning cut accuracy and raise language-prior reliance [23]. Beyond showing that CoT hurts, we rule out format and visual forgetting, localize where rationale turns against the image, and decompose the benchmark-level change into helpful shortcut dilution and harmful valid-cue loss, showing that CoTDirect tracks written-relation accuracy minus Direct accuracy. CoT losses concentrate on tasks where verbalizing impairs humans [33]; we locate this cost in the written relation. As benchmarks carry non-visual shortcuts [8, 16], we perturb cues in conflict as in depth psychophysics [26] and shapetexture tests [15]. Faithfulness, snowballing, and grounding. Traces can rationalize answers [2, 43] or compute in filler [37], while VLM probes show yes bias [31] and contrastive decoding counters priors via distorted images [28]. Lanham et al. [27] test faithfulness through early answering and mistake injection. We refine early answering to identify the commit sentence where an initially correct forced readout turns wrong, and we edit perceptual claims whose ground truth is fixed by the rendered scene. Unlike sentence ranking by resampled rollouts [7], post-answer rationalization in LLMs [53], or acceptance of earlier hallucinations [55], we locate without resampling the sentence where rationale turns against the image, before any answer token, and test 3 image use after it via twin swaps. Zhao et al. [54] inject misleading captions and wrong-think prefixes into RL-tuned VLMs; we show that unperturbed VLMs write their own false spatial claims and obey them. Forgetting, probes, and explicit state. Against falling image attention in long chains, TVC [39] re-injects visual tokens and VAPO [40] and Remember-R1 [10] reward grounding; in short CoT, re-showing the image does not recover accuracy. Mechanistic studies examine linear spatial IDs [24]: Fu et al. [13] show that VLMs encode visual features unused in direct answers, and Wang and Xu [46] ask whether spatial encodings reach the output. Complementing these findings, we show that VLM can write false spatial relation even while probe at the relation token still decodes the true depth order, and we pinpoint where in the rationale visual information stops governing the answer. Our probe follows truthfulness probing [3, 9, 35], where models encode the truth yet output an error [36], and activation steering [29]. Explicit visual state (crops [48], sketchpads [20], harnesses [18]) replaces prose; our structured state encodes the height shortcut rather than occlusion (Sec. 9 and Tab. S28). 3. It therefore acts as sizeconfounded stress test, and we analyze its 431 visibly overlapping scenes. Text lock-in is therefore avoidable at the answer step, motivating answer-step re-grounding as concrete target for open VLMs. 9. Towards Answer-Step Re-grounding Because open VLMs retain the true relation in mid-layer representations (Sec. 5) and frontier models show that text lock-in is avoidable (Sec. 8), we test whether label-free inference-time interventions can break lock-in and whether answer-step re-grounding can be learned directly. 9.1. Label-free inference-time interventions No label-free inference-time intervention we tested beats Direct on average on its evaluated sets (or out of sample where tested; Tab. 14). Full per-model tables and controls are in Appendix F. Commit-sentence gate. Replacing the oracle claim edit of Sec. 6 with label-free criterion, the commit-sentence gate (Tab. S27) tracks the turn-closed forced readout Pj(d) of the models own Direct answer after each sentence sj (no gold labels enter). Whenever sj drops (d) from 0.5 to < 0.5, the gate resamples sj up to = 4 times at = 0.7, keeping the first sample that preserves (d) 0.5 or dropping sj and re-gating the continuation if all flip (at most 8 gate events per item, reached by at most 7.7% of items). Across four models and three synthetic sets, the gate recovers +9.8 to +21.8 points over CoT in the six cells where CoT loses significantly, outperforming rule-parsed text gate by 4.610.9 points. However, it never significantly beats Direct (6.4 to +0.6 points, CI below zero in 5/12 cells), discards 59%96% of CoTs rescues, costs 2.55.0 CoTs tokens plus 825 forced readouts per item, and where CoT gains on the cue set and twins it drops 2.95.0 points below CoT by restoring Directs lower-is-closer prior rather than occlusion. Count-matched controls confirm that the gate acts as Direct with rationale attached (Appendix F.1, which also reports post-hoc answer-first explanations). Structured spatial state. To test whether replacing free prose with structured schema avoids transcription errors, we prompt the assistant to complete JSON object naming both objects, their bounding boxes, which object is occluded, and which is in front ( 300 tokens) before the same-turn readout (Tab. S28). The schema parses on 97% 100% of items and recovers +13.2 to +19.6 points of the free-CoT loss on Synthetic Depth in five models, but stays below Direct in Qwen2.5-VL-3B (13.2) and InternVL3-8B (7.2). On the occlusion twins, it removes the CoT loss in Molmo-7B-D (+1.24 over CoT) but lowers below free CoT in Qwen3-VL-8B (0.62) and Phi-3.5-Vision (0.38). The front field is correct on 49.6%72.6% of twin images and names the upper object as front in 19.9%45.9% (against 50/50 design), showing that the structured state largely encodes the loweris-closer heuristic rather than occlusion perception. Body-relation readout and additional label-free controls. Because Stage-3 conclusion mis-mapping costs accuracy on the cue set, we tested pre-specified label-free readout that answers deterministically from the last body relation (twojudge consensus on conclusion-removed text, falling back to CoT in BRC or Direct in BRD when no relation is stated; Tab. S29). In sample on the cue set, BRC beats Direct 17 Table 14. Summary of label-free inference-time interventions against Direct. S30), order-swap probability averaging (gains held-out Direct in 3/7 models), and frozen Direct-margin gating (Tab. 14). 9.2. Learning answer-step re-grounding (pilot) Since inference-time interventions do not supply answerstep image checking, we test whether re-grounding is learnable in pre-specified single-model pilot (H1H4) on Qwen3-VL-8B (Tab. 15). We LoRA-fine-tune the model (rank 16, one epoch, loss on the answer letter only) on its own conclusion-removed rationales for newly rendered scenes (1,512 occlusion-twin pairs and 1,008 left/right mirror pairs, with no overlap with any evaluation image). Both training arms use 5,040 examples with labels always determined by the shown image: the counterfactual arm (CF) pairs one rationale per scene pair (2,520 rationales) with both images so that half of training examples contradict the text, whereas the matched control (MATCH) pairs each of the 5,040 rationales with its own image (which still contradicts the image label on 13.3% of examples where the base models rationale was wrong). Because the CV-Bench left- /right template and mirroring appear in rendered training, mirrored CV-Bench tests transfer to the natural-image domain rather than new question template. Fine-tuning on rendered scenes alone restores answerstep image use on natural photographs (Tab. 15). With the base models Rcut held fixed (H1), the twin image effect rises from 2.9 to 51.7 (MATCH) and 58.9 (CF) on COCO occlusion twins and from 1.3 to 90.7 and 93.4 on mirrored CV-Bench. On the pooled 4,015-item natural set (H2), Direct accuracy rises from 81.3% to 84.4% (MATCH, +3.1) and 84.2% (CF, +2.9 [+2.0, +3.9]). On the heldout pool, Direct accuracy reaches 70.0% (MATCH) and 68.8% (CF, 1.8 [4.4, +0.5]). On the main pool (H3, where the pilots base re-run has CoTDirect = 3.0 vs. 3.5 in Tab. 2), the CoT loss disappears (0.1 MATCH, +0.1 CF). At the same time, retention of base-correct D+C+ held-out answers (n = 469) moves from 98.9% to 96.2% (MATCH) and 92.8% (CF, 6.2 [8.7, 3.9]). Counterfactual pairing adds little re-grounding over MATCH (+7.2 [+5.0, +9.5] on COCO, +2.6 [+0.0, +6.0] on CV-Bench; H1 partial) while altering how the text is used when the image is uninformative. Under uniform gray image (H4), MATCH still follows the base rationales written relation on 83.7% of COCO twins and 95.9% of mirrored CV-Bench items (base: 96.3% and 100.0%), whereas CF drops to 65.6% and 57.1%; on the rendered training domain both arms fall to 43.0%67.3%, so the pooled H4 endpoint is not met (68.7% MATCH, 47.3% CF). On natural photographs, MATCH therefore consults the image when it is informative and follows the rationale when it is not, whereas counterfactual pairing mainly teaches the model to discount the text. This single-model pilot suggests that answer-step regrounding is learnable from fixed rationales with imagedetermined labels on rendered scenes without requiring contradicting twin pairs. 10. Discussion Why benchmarks miss the failure. Shortcut relief and lost valid cues offset each other on average, so standard aggregate scores on natural benchmarks often show small or null net CoTDirect gap despite heavy item-level answer churn (Tabs. 10 and S12b). Controlled cue conflicts and fixed-rationale counterfactual image swaps expose that the 18 Table 15. Pre-specified LoRA pilot of the re-grounding recipe (Qwen3-VL-8B). Implications for open VLMs. Open models already hold the required perceptual signal: the true depth order remains decodable at the written relation token (Sec. 5 and Tab. S16), and rationale-body checkers use the image to reject an appended wrong conclusion (Sec. 6, Fig. 5, and Tab. S3). What open VLMs lack is an answer step that re-consults the image when it conflicts with their own generated text. Prompting and inference-time heuristics do not supply this behavior: across re-shown images or questions, perception-first instructions, structured JSON state, body-relation readouts, and commit-sentence gating, none beats Direct on average on its evaluated sets (or out of sample where tested; Sec. 9 and Tab. 14). By contrast, an unconditional oracle edit replacing the first claim with the true relation beats Direct by 14.334.9 points in five of six core models tested (Molmo-7B-D 12.3; Sec. 6 and Tab. 7). Three of six frontier closed models show that answer-step regrounding is achievable, though in those APIs it is confounded with answer-turn reasoning (Sec. 8), and our prespecified single-model LoRA pilot suggests that fine-tuning on fixed rationales with image-determined labels (MATCH) restores answer-step re-grounding on natural photographs from rendered scenes alone (Sec. 9.2). Combining answerstep re-grounding with reinforcement learning rewards for visually consistent intermediate claims [10, 52] is natural next step. 11. Conclusion We showed that short chain-of-thought turns spatial VQA from perception problem into transcription problem. Writing re-weights visual cues and produces false spatial relations, the forced readout then locks onto the written text instead of the image across both rendered scenes and natural photographs, and concluding sentences can mis-map even true relations on converse questions. Consequently, written-relation accuracy minus Direct accuracy accounts for when CoT helps or hurts. Model scale alone does not remove this bottleneck, and label-free inference-time interventions do not beat Direct on average out of sample. Answer-step re-grounding, observed in three of six frontier closed models and demonstrated in our single-model LoRA pilot on natural photographs, offers direct path to breaking text lock-in.

sections.content: Reading guide. Appendix details the models, prompts, engines, and statistical tests, along with truncation-rule definitions (Appendix A.1), the occlusion rule and heuristic baselines (Appendices A.2 and A.3), sentence judges (Appendix A.4), frozen held-out protocol details (Appendix A.5), and closed-model API settings supporting Sec. 8 (Appendix A.6). Appendices to supplement Analyses 14 of the main paper. Specifically, we cover format controls and answer churn (Appendix B), commit-sentence checks, the full Qwen3-VL-32B pipeline, uniform-attenuation tests, probes, and steering (Appendix C). We then report phrasingform claim edits, attention-edge knockouts, body-vs.-image checking, and regenerated closed-model controls (Appendix D), followed by full two-channel, larger/reasoningtuned cohort, closed-model, and multi-image benchmark tables (Appendix E). Appendix supplements Sec. 9 with full per-model tables for the label-free interventions, gate controls, answer-first explanations, perception-first prompts, order swaps, and margin gating, and Appendix provides reproducibility notes, verbatim prompts, and model checkpoints. Tab. S1 maps each claim of the main paper to its supporting evidence, and Tab. S5 reports the 95% CIs for every cell of main Tab. 1. Additional per-model breakdowns and per-item outputs are available in the released repository (github.com/MING-ZCH/seeing-right-writing-wrong). Appendix summary tables. Tabs. S1 to S5 collect the evidence map, main-pool task breakdown, conclusion-removed attention knockouts, Synthetic Depth leverage checks, and per-cell CIs for Tab. 1; additional supporting tables (Tab. S6 onward) follow in their respective sections. Glossary. DC: Direct correct (+) or wrong () and CoT correct or wrong on the same item (e.g., D+C). Occlusion-competent (main paper: passes the occlusion-reading rule): Direct cue-set accuracy CI low > 70% and occlusion weight CI low > 0 (Appendix A.2). pair: pair-matched sensitivity from both queries of an image or twin pair, ln[(nBC + 0.5)/(nBW + 0.5)]/1.702. j: commit sentence, the first sentence after which forced-readout (gold) falls below 0.5 and stays there. S16). 23 A. Implementation, Stimuli, and Judges Models, engines, and image budgets. All open models use bfloat16 with greedy decoding (temperature 0), prefix caching, and seed 0. Qwen2.5-VL-3B/7B [5], InternVL3-8B [56], and Phi-3.5-Vision [1] run on the vLLM 0.8.4 V0 engine [25] (12,288-token context, up to two images per prompt), whereas Molmo-7B-D [12] uses the V1 engine of the same version (4,096-token Qwen3-VL-8B (Instruct context, one image slot). and Thinking) and InternVL3.5-8B run on vLLM 0.11 (V1 only). Per-image visual budgets follow each models standard configuration: at most 1280 28 28 pixels for the Qwen2.5-VL models (vLLM 0.11 ignores max_pixels for Qwen3-VL, which therefore ran at its processor default; the rendered sets and COCO twins are 1 MP and unaffected), up to 6 dynamic tiles for the InternVL models (max_dynamic_patch=6), and 4 crops for Phi-3.5-Vision (num_crops=4). S10a) has CI lower bound above 0; CIs resample twin pairs, and Qwen3-VL-8B-Thinking, whose cue-set run was added later, is evaluated in Tab. S22. The rule was fixed in the analysis code before the per-model table was produced; the cue-set accuracies had been reported in earlier analyses, so the rule is explicit but not blind. Any accuracy threshold on the CI lower bound above 60.8% (InternVL3-8B) and below 77.0% (Qwen3-VL-8B) gives the same split of the seven instruct models, and criterion (ii) holds for all seven. Synthetic Depth: overlapping images and pairmatched sensitivity. Of the 500 Synthetic Depth images, 431 show visible overlap, 40 only touch or are separated (gold follows size), and 29 are nearly fully hidden. The main text analyzes the 431; Tab. S9a gives both. On the 431, pair falls with CI below zero in four models (0.78 to 1.55) against six on all 500: Qwen2.5-VL-7B (0.14 [0.30, +0.03]) and Phi-3.5-Vision (0.21 [0.40, +0.00]) lose significance, and InternVL3.5-8B still rises (+0.19). Pooled falls in six models on both sets (0.38 to 1.89 on the 431), and the commit audit is unchanged (184/209 = 88.0% vs. 19/203 = 9.4%). Each image yields one of four answer pairs under the two object orders: both orders correct (BC), yes to both (YY, affirming both queried relations), no to both (NN), or both wrong (BW, consistent reversed percept). We assume (yes) = σ(bi /2) for image under the two orders, with free per-image bias bi and sensitivity that is constant over images, and conditionally independent answers. Then nBC/nBW estimates whatever the bi, and pair = ln[(nBC + 0.5)/(nBW + 0.5)]/1.702 is pair-matched (conditional-logit) sensitivity on the probit scale that, under this common-sensitivity model, removes any per-image bias, including affirmation. Under CoT, pair falls in six models, with CIs below zero (0.16 to 1.50), and rises in InternVL3.5-8B (+0.20; Tab. S9b). The common-sensitivity model is testable: with common , the share of images answered differently under the two orders, BC+BW, cannot exceed σ(/2)2 + σ(/2)2. Under Direct the observed share exceeds this bound in four models (Qwen2.5-VL-7B, InternVL3-8B, Phi-3.5-Vision, Molmo-7B-D), so sensitivity varies across images, and pair is then biasweighted mean of image-level sensitivities, which bias shift could lower by moving easy images out of the discordant set. We therefore fix the stratum weights across arms (size-standardised pair): over visible-area-ratio terciles it falls in five of seven models and over quintiles in six, and InternVL3.5-8B rises in both (+0.20). By tercile, pair falls significantly in 1, 5, and 4 of seven models (low, mid, high ratio), so the loss concentrates on sizeasymmetric pairs. logistic mixed model with an image random sensitivity slope, which does not assume common sensitivity, is weakly identified with two answers per image and arm; its mean falls with CI below zero in three of seven models (Qwen2.5-VL-3B, Qwen2.5-VL-7B, InternVL3-8B) and is indeterminate in the other four. A.3. Cue-factorial set and cue weights The cue-factorial set crosses two size conditions (front/back area ratio 1.251.80 or 0.550.80) with two vertical conditions (front object lower or higher in the image), with 100 base scenes per cell and an identity-swapped twin for each (800 images, 1,600 prompts with both phrasings), so occlusion is the only valid cue. The main text reports probit GLM fit (component = 2β, weak (0, 10) prior, twin-pair bootstrap; no separation in any open model on the cue set; Tab. S10a). per-cell decomposition of pooled into occlusion, vertical, and size components agrees with the GLM in sign for every component, within 0.34 for the occlusion component and within 0.53 for the vertical component. The GLM occlusion loss has CI below zero in all seven open models and survives BenjaminiHochberg control with resampling in all seven; with Wald (bootstrap SE) it survives in six, as the Qwen2.5-VL-7B loss (0.34 [0.76, 0.07]) misses (q = 0.053 vs. 0.020). DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash is run with reasoning_effort=none in both arms (the analysis uses the 1,566 prompts answered in both arms) and is near separation under Direct (89.5% 90.7% accuracy under CoT), so its occlusion CI is wide. If CoT only added image-independent Scale-free check. variance, all probit cue weights would shrink by one factor; common factor fit over the three cue weights gives = 0.270.55. Tab. S10b therefore reports each cues average marginal effect (AME) on the probability that the answer calls the queried subject the front shape (same probit model, points; 1,000 twin-pair bootstrap draws, Direct and CoT resampled jointly), which is our primary cueeffect scale (Tabs. 1, 3 and S22 to S24). First CoT claims (rule parser v3, which skips symmetric verbs such as overlaps and handles negation) name the lower shape in 40.4% (Qwen3-VL-8B) to 65.1%66.4% (InternVL3.5-8B, Qwen2.5-VL-7B) of parsed claims, so the lower-is-closer prior is adopted in writing by some models and reversed by others; Qwen3-VL-8Bs on top claims name the upper shape in 88.6% of cases. logistic model of which shape claim names as front gives questionaffirming term that is positive in six models (+0.21 to +1.22, CIs above zero) and negative in Qwen2.5-VL-7B (0.61 [0.74, 0.49]); on 560 judge-labelled claims it stays above zero under judge, rule-v2, and rule-v3 labels in those six (marginally in InternVL3.5-8B) and is not robust in Qwen2.5-VL-7B, so we claim affirmation only for the six. On the original twins, whose front shape is never drawn larger, pooled falls under CoT in Phi-3.5-Vision, Molmo-7B-D, Qwen3-VL-8B, and Qwen3-VL-8B-Thinking and rises in InternVL3-8B (+0.43), InternVL3.5-8B (+0.25), and Qwen2.5-VL-7B (+0.21; not significant after FDR control); these three have strong Direct loweris-closer prior, which the balanced front-above/below design turns into noise, so diluting the prior raises marginal without adding occlusion signal. A.4. Sentence judges For each model we take the stored greedy rationale of every Synthetic Depth item in the D+C and D+C+ groups and extract the first sentence that names both shapes together with an occlusion or depth verb (overlap, cover, on top of, obscure, block, in front of, or passive form such as covered by, behind); sentences that pose question (whether, if the, determine, asks) are skipped. We sample up to 40 parsed sentences per model and group (seed 0) and send each sentence together with the image to two judges, Claude Opus 5.5 (reasoning_effort=high) and GPT-6-Astra, with the prompt: Here is an image and one sentence that model wrote about it: {sentence}. Consider only what the sentence claims about which shape is in front of, on top of, covering, or overlapping the other. Does that claim match the image? Reply with exactly one word: correct, incorrect, or unclear. Tab. S11 reports the share judged incorrect among sentences judge does not label unclear, with Wilson 95% intervals. The two judges agree on 96.1% of the sentences both label (κ = 0.92). rule-based parse agrees with them on 75.3% (κ = 0.51) and 79.2% (κ = 0.59); it misses negations such as not in front of. Fig. 1b plots the two-judge consensus (58.3%97.4% on D+C, 5.4%25.7% on D+C+, 11.5% 35.9% on DC+). In blind cross-check of 120 first claims (60 from Synthetic Depth, 60 from natural images) by three model reviewers (Claude Opus 5.5, Gemini-4-Argon, Gemini-4-Carbon), the majority label agrees with the Claude Opus 5.5 judge on 94.3% (κ = 0.89) and with the GPT-6Astra judge on 95.4% (κ = 0.91); this is model crosscheck, not human validation. On stratified 30-sentence sample (12 D+C commit, 12 matched relational D+C+, and 6 rescue sentences; seven models), human labels (one annotator, the author, blind to model, DC cell, and judge labels) agree with the judge consensus on 23 of 24 sentences that both label as consistent or contradicting (κ = 0.91; judgejudge κ = 0.84 on the same sample). The same two models also serve as text-only judges that extract which relation rationale states; their agreement is given with each analysis. A.5. Held-out pool and frozen protocol The held-out pool has 767 binary items: BLINK val Spatial Relation (143) and Relative Depth (124), and five 3DSRBench COCO categories with 100 items each (one item per image, seed 0). For each model, before the held-out CoT, vote, and description runs, we wrote one time-stamped file (released with the outputs) that contains (i) the Directmargin gate thresholds τ selected by 5-fold cross-validation on the main pool, (ii) item-level and constant-p predictions of 4-sample majority voting (T = 0.7) for every held-out task and for the pooled set, computed from held-out Direct probabilities, and (iii) SHA-256 hashes of the Direct outputs, the τ file, and the code. These two predictions (gate transfer and vote accuracy) are the only frozen endpoints; the BLINK Relative Depth comparison was not prespecified endpoint. The item-level vote prediction matches observed voting within 0.31.5 points in six models and 2.1 points in Molmo-7B-D, while the constant-p baseline overestimates voting by up to 8.5 points; the frozen gate gives 0.8 to +2.1 over Direct with every CI including zero. Cross-model notes. Per-task accuracies and main crossmodel differences are reported in Sec. 7 (Tab. 10). Crossmodel bootstrap intervals resample items with the set of models fixed, so they describe these models. On the post hoc 324-item depth-valid subset, CoT Direct is 3.5 [6.1, 1.0] over eight open models and CoT Filler+turn is 3.4 [6.1, 0.6] over the seven instruct models (no single per-model CI excludes zero); 3DSRBench closer (1.5) and in front of (1.1) do not change reliably, and below-chance Direct accuracy on 3DSR Left (28%41%) suggests that models answer in the cameras frame rather than the objects own frame. 31 Table S10. Direct appends Answer with the options letter only.; CoT asks the model to describe what it sees, reason, and end with Answer: (X) (Appendix G.1). Because these APIs return no option log-probabilities, we report answer-level metrics parsed from each reply, queried once at the providers default temperature. GPT-6-Astra has 122 BLINK Relative Depth items because the providers content-safety filter rejected two images (HTTP 400) in both conditions. On the hard occlusion set (144 base pairs plus twins, 576 prompts per condition across three difficulty levels with thin overlap slivers, low contrast, distractor shapes, blur, noise, and smaller objects), hard-set accuracies count failed replies as wrong (HY4 67.9%; 69.2% on items with both replies). Perception-first prompts, order swaps, and margin gating Perception-first prompts. We pre-specified three labelfree replacements of the assistant prefix Lets think step by step.: P1 (primary), First, look at where the two shapes overlap and say which shapes outline is complete there (that shape is in front). Then answer.; P2, which restates the question first; and P3, which does both. The primary endpoint, P1Direct averaged over the seven open models on the cue set and on BLINK Relative Depth plus CV-Bench 3D Depth (724 items), required both CI lower bounds above zero. As the main paper argues, prompting does not supply answer-step re-grounding: P1Direct is 4.2 [5.6, 2.8] and 2.1 [3.0, 1.2], and no prompt beats Direct pooled on any set. Because several models end the turn right after that instruction, we pre-specified second test (Tab. S30): the perception-first instruction is appended to the question in the user turn (natural images: look for depth cues for the two marked points or objects . . . and state which is closer), and the assistant turn starts with the usual Lets think step by step. (U1); U2 adds reminder to check which object and which relation the question asks about. Every model now writes (empty continuations 0% in all modelset cells except Phi-3.5-Vision on BLINK, whose plain CoT there is also empty). The pre-specified primary is not met: U1Direct is 4.5 [6.3, 2.6] on the cue set and 4.4 [5.7, 3.2] on BLINK + CV-Bench, no model beats Direct on natural images, and the gain over CoT there vanishes (+0.8 [0.4, +2.0]; P1 had +3.1, mostly from empty continuations). The two cue-set gains (Qwen2.5-VL-7B +3.8, InternVL3.5-8B +4.6) equal those models own CoT gains. Molmo-7B-D loses 27.2 points: it writes that the queried shapes outline is complete and answers yes (written relation 63.8% correct vs. 80.8% under CoT); the reminder (U2) helps in one of four occlusion readers. Order swaps and margin gating. Averaging original and optionor object-order-swapped probabilities lifts main-pool Sym-Direct in 6/7 models (+0.3 to +4.2) but held-out Direct in only 3/7. Routing items with (A)P (B) < τ to CoT (τ chosen by 5-fold cross-validation on the main pool) gains +1.1 to +2.5 in-sample (4/7 models), yet the frozen held-out τ gives 0.8 to +2.1 over Direct with every CI including zero. Flagging CoT answer when CoT gives different answers on the original and the orderswapped prompt catches 36.9%59.4% of main-pool CoT errors but only 18.1%34.9% held out (held-out precision 43.5%55.9%).
